title: Annotation on the Chapter on the Lower Grade, Lower Birth of the Sūtra of Contemplation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, spoken by the Buddha (abbreviated as the Sūtra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, or the Contemplation Sūtra), is one of the Three Pure Land Sūtras.

inline.s: The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, spoken by the Buddha (abbreviated as the Sūtra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, or the Contemplation Sūtra), is one of the Three Pure Land Sūtras.

[The Three Pure Land Sūtras] The three scriptures on which the Pure Land school relies, namely the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sūtra.

The content of this sūtra relates how King Bimbisāra met with calamity within his own household and was imprisoned by his rebellious son Ajātaśatru. His consort Vaidehī secretly went to the place of imprisonment and offered King Bimbisāra ghee and honey mixed with roasted barley flour, together with grape juice. After the king had eaten, his strength gradually recovered. Clasping his palms in reverence, he paid homage from afar to Śākyamuni Buddha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and begged him to send Mahāmaudgalyāyana to confer upon him the eight precepts. The World-Honored One, besides sending the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, also sent the venerable Pūrṇa to speak the Dharma to the great king.

[The eight precepts] Also called the fast of the eight precepts (ba guan zhai jie). First, not to take life — not to kill any living animal. Second, not to take what is not given — not to take what others have not given. Third, not to engage in non-brahmacarya — not to engage in sexual union. Fourth, not to speak falsely — not to speak words contrary to fact. Fifth, not to drink alcohol — not to drink any kind of intoxicating liquor. Sixth, not to adorn with garlands, or to dance, sing, and listen to music — that is, not to anoint the body with fragrance or deck it with flower garlands (wreaths), and not to watch dancing or hear songs. Seventh, not to sleep or sit on a high, broad, ornate bed — that is, not to lie or sit on a high, broad, and splendid bed. Eighth, not to eat at improper times — that is, not to eat food at the wrong time, that is, not to eat after noon.

Thus twenty-one days passed. King Bimbisāra had food to eat and had heard the Dharma, so his body and mind were sound and healthy. Ajātaśatru came to ask the gatekeeper whether his father was still alive. The gatekeeper then reported to Ajātaśatru that Queen Vaidehī had brought the king food, and that the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and others had come through the air to confer the precepts on the king and to speak the Dharma. Ajātaśatru then turned his anger upon his mother, Queen Vaidehī, and seizing a sharp sword sought to kill her. Only after the ministers Candraprabha and Jīvaka and others remonstrated with him did he change to imprisoning his mother.

After Queen Vaidehī was imprisoned, she was deeply distressed, weeping and shedding tears like rain, and from afar called upon Śākyamuni Buddha who was then on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. The Buddha, knowing what was in Vaidehī's mind, led Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda in person to the palace. Queen Vaidehī expressed to the Buddha that she no longer wished to remain in this defiled and evil Sahā world. The Buddha then manifested the pure and wondrous lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions so that Queen Vaidehī might choose the place of her rebirth. After Queen Vaidehī had chosen the Western Pure Land, the Buddha first told her that those who wish to be reborn in the Western Pure Land should
cultivate the three meritorious deeds of pure karma:
"Those who wish to be reborn in that land
(the Western Pure Land)

should cultivate the three meritorious deeds: first, to be filial to one's parents, to serve one's teachers and elders, to be kind and not to kill, and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; second, to receive and hold the Three Refuges, to be complete in all the precepts, and not to violate dignified deportment; third, to arouse the bodhi-mind, to believe deeply in cause and effect, to recite and read the Mahāyāna, and to encourage and advance fellow practitioners."
Then

she laid out the sequence of the sixteen contemplations, explaining to her the way to be reborn in the Western Pure Land. Among these she mentioned the stages of rebirth in the three grades (upper, middle, lower) and the nine classes.
[The sixteen contemplations] The sixteen contemplations: (
) the contemplation of the sun: with single-minded attention contemplate the setting sun of the West, hanging like a drum. (
) the contemplation of water: with a clear mind contemplate the waters of the West forming ice, pure and luminous, like crystal. (
) the contemplation of the ground: with one mind contemplate the pure crystal ground of the land of ultimate bliss, radiant within and without, pure and majestic. (
) the contemplation of the trees: with one mind contemplate the seven rows of trees, composed of manifold gems, with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits interwoven with the eight treasures. (

) the contemplation of the pools: with focused attention contemplate the pool of the seven jewels, where the water of the eight virtues, like wish-fulfilling jewels, flows and pours among the flowers. (

) the general contemplation: with one mind contemplate the land of ultimate bliss, formed of all kinds of jewels, with pavilions, terraces, and towers, where the deities gather, performing celestial music, always mindful of the Three Jewels. (

) the contemplation of the lotus seat: with one mind contemplate above the pool of seven jewels the platform of a hundred gems, the wondrous net of genuine pearls, and the adorned vajra-seat, transformed at will, performing great Buddha-deeds. (

) the contemplation of the sacred images: with one mind contemplate Amitābha Buddha seated upon the lotus platform, with the two great bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta standing in attendance on either side, emitting great light that shines throughout the ten directions. The waters, the birds, and the trees all speak the wondrous Dharma. (

) the contemplation of the Buddha's body: with one mind contemplate the marks and light of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life — the curl of white hair that revolves over five Sumerus, the deep blue eyes clear as the four great seas. Within the marks of his body, see throughout the countless Buddhas of the ten directions. (

) the contemplation of Avalokiteshvara: with one mind contemplate the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara with his flesh-colored topknot and encircling halo, his purple-golden body, adorned with excellent marks, at ease in transformations, filling the whole Dharma-realm. (

) the contemplation of Mahasthamaprapta: with one mind contemplate the bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta with his purple-golden body, his encircling halo universally shining; within the light of a single pore see the countless Buddhas of the ten directions. When the bodhisattva walks, the worlds of the ten directions all quake. (

) the contemplation of the general aspiration: with one mind contemplate oneself already reborn in the Western Pure Land, seated cross-legged within a lotus flower. When the lotus opens, five hundred colored lights touch my body, and I see Buddhas and bodhisattvas filling the sky. The waters, birds, trees, and groves and the sounds emitted by the Buddhas all proclaim the wondrous Dharma. (

) the contemplation of mixed imagery: with one mind contemplate Amitābha Buddha, at ease in his spiritual powers, appearing in the lands of the ten directions according to their kind, with the Three Sages appearing together, great and small without impediment, seated on the jeweled lotus. (14) the contemplation of the upper grade of birth: with one mind contemplate the rebirth-conditions, the circumstances of rebirth, and the benefits after birth of the three types — the upper-grade upper birth, the upper-grade middle birth, and the upper-grade lower birth. (15) the contemplation of the middle grade of birth: with one mind contemplate the rebirth-conditions, the circumstances of rebirth, and the benefits after birth of the three types — the middle-grade upper, the middle-grade middle, and the middle-grade lower. (16) the contemplation of the lower grade of birth: with one mind contemplate the rebirth-conditions, the circumstances of rebirth, and the benefits after birth of the three types — the lower-grade upper, the lower-grade middle, and the lower-grade lower.

This essay concerns the chapter on the lower grade, lower birth in the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. In this chapter the World-Honored One reveals: for a person who has committed the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds,
if at death the ten thoughts continue without break
he will at once attain
the extinction of his offenses
and rebirth; his grade is the lower grade, lower birth.
Here is the commentary:
[A person of the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds, if at death the ten thoughts continue without break, at once attains the extinction of offenses and rebirth] Master Daochuo taught:
"If there is a sentient being,
even if he has committed evil throughout his life, at the end of his life, with ten thoughts continuing without break, calling upon my name,
if he is not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
(see
Master Daochuo's Pure Land Teaching

[The Buddha said to Ānanda and Vaidehī: For the lower grade, lower birth — there may be sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds, who commit the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds and are possessed of all manner of unwholesomeness. Such foolish persons, on account of their evil karma, should fall into the evil destinies and pass through many kalpas, suffering endlessly.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda and Queen Vaidehī: For the lower grade, lower birth — if there are sentient beings who commit evil karma, who commit the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds, doing all manner of things. Such foolish persons, because of the evil karma, should fall into the evil destinies and pass through many kalpas, suffering endlessly.

[The five grave offenses] Killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, splitting the harmonious Saṃgha, and causing blood to flow from the Buddha's body. Because these violate and betray grace and virtue, they are called the five grave offenses. [The ten evil deeds] Also called the ten unwholesome deeds: taking life, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle chatter, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and ignorance.

[When such a foolish person is at the end of his life, he meets a good spiritual friend who comforts him in various ways, speaks the wondrous Dharma for him, and instructs him to contemplate the Buddha. That person, pressed by suffering, has no leisure to contemplate the Buddha. The good friend says to him: "If you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should call upon the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Thus with utmost sincerity, let the sound be unbroken — being complete in ten thoughts — calling upon "Namo Amitābha Buddha.""]

When such a foolish person is at the end of his life, he meets a good spiritual friend who comforts him in various ways and speaks to him of the splendor of the Western Pure Land and the great benefit of rebirth there, and instructs him to contemplate Amitābha Buddha so as to be reborn there. Since the marks of hell appear before this person, he has no leisure to still his mind and contemplate the Buddha; so the good friend tells him: "If you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should call upon that Buddha's name. With a pure, unbroken mind, with utmost sincerity, call upon "Namo Amitābha Buddha," thought after thought continuing, complete in ten sounds."

[Instructing him to contemplate the Buddha] Here this means teaching him to contemplate Amitābha Buddha. The word "contemplate" (nian) here means to be mindful and to form the visualization. [Pressed by suffering] The marks of hell appear. [No leisure] No free time. [If you cannot contemplate that Buddha, you should call upon the Buddha of Immeasurable Life] This sūtra (the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life) mainly discusses contemplation-recitation, so the term "contemplating the Buddha" refers to contemplation-recitation, while the recitation of the name is called "calling upon the Buddha." [Thus with utmost sincerity, let the sound be unbroken] Pure and undivided is called "utmost sincerity"; continuing unbroken into a whole is why it is "unbroken." [Ten thoughts] This means ten sounds of the Buddha-name.
Please pay special attention to this passage:
"Thus with utmost sincerity, let the sound be unbroken, being complete in ten thoughts, calling upon "Namo Amitābha Buddha.""
In the passage,
thus with utmost sincerity
means to reach the highest purity and sincerity, without any stray thought;
let the sound be unbroken
means the Buddha-name continues without interruption;
being complete in ten thoughts, calling upon "Namo Amitābha Buddha"
means having completed ten utterances of "Namo Amitābha Buddha." Because these three conditions are fulfilled — that is, having accomplished
the ten thoughts continuing without break at death
— only then does such an evil person attain
the extinction of
the offenses of birth and death of eighty koṭis of kalpas and be reborn in the Western Pure Land.
The Two Gateways of Resolving Doubt and Aspiration for Rebirth in the Pure Land says:
"Though originally an evil-doer,
with ten thoughts of utmost sincerity
he is reborn in that land."
[Because he calls upon the Buddha's name, within thought after thought the offenses of birth and death of eighty koṭis of kalpas are extinguished.]
Because he thus calls upon the Buddha's name with ten thoughts continuing without break, within thought after thought the offenses of birth and death of eighty koṭis of kalpas are extinguished.
Regarding the circumstances of a person of the lower grade, lower birth reciting the Buddha at death and attaining rebirth, Master Yinguang taught:
"The Contemplation Sūtra [speaks of] the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds. When such a person is about to die, the marks of hell appear, and there is a good spiritual friend
(original note: This is without regard to monk or layman, man or woman; whoever can teach that person to recite the Buddha is called a good spiritual friend.)

who teaches him to recite the Buddha — it may be only ten sounds, or even fewer than ten sounds — and when he straightway dies, he may still rely on the Buddha's compassionate power and be reborn while carrying his karma. These ten thoughts, compared with ordinary ten thoughts, have a power of intensity that differs as heaven from the deep, which is why he attains rebirth. Pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, the moment he hears the Buddha's name he invokes it with his whole being.

Apart from this recitation, there is absolutely no other thought. And though he has not personally realized single-minded concentration, still his heart is at bottom without a single differing thought.
The Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, Third Series
Volume Two
Letter in Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru
Master Shandao's Commentary on the Four Fascicles of the Contemplation Sūtra explains the meaning of the "lower grade, lower birth" chapter:

"From "such a foolish person" down to "offenses of birth and death," it is just clarifying that upon hearing the Dharma and reciting the Buddha one obtains a present benefit, and there are ten points: first, clarifying the person who committed evil again; second, clarifying that his life-span will not last long; third, clarifying that at death he meets a good spiritual friend; fourth, clarifying that the good person comforts and instructs him to recite the Buddha; fifth, clarifying that the sinful person is pressed by the suffering of death and has no way to recite the Buddha's name; sixth, clarifying that the good friend, knowing his suffering and loss of mindfulness, turns to teaching him to call aloud the name of Amitābha; seventh, clarifying how many the recitations,
sound after sound without interruption
; eighth, clarifying the removal of offenses of many kalpas; ninth,
clarifying that with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus comes in response
(indicating: with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus comes in response)
; tenth, clarifying the slowness or swiftness of the departure, arriving straightway at the land of return."
Please note especially what Master Shandao says here:
rebirth through right mindfulness at death

("with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus comes in response"). Yet the Primal Vow teaching, which mouths at every turn that it "relies on Master Shandao," resolutely opposes rebirth through right mindfulness at death!
Please note especially what Master Shandao says in his instruction: "
sound after sound without interruption
and "
with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus comes to welcome
Since it is "right mindfulness at death," this shows that when reciting the Buddha at death there is no deluded thought mixed in. Since there is no deluded thought mixed in, therefore the
sound after sound without interruption

" here is the recitation-thought of the Buddha, thought after thought continuing. And so this person of the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds at death recites the Buddha with thought after thought continuing — right mindfulness at death — and thus extinguishes his offenses and attains rebirth.
On this point, Master Daochuo also taught in the Compendium of Peace and Bliss (Anle Ji):
At the time of death of all sentient beings
the sword-wind dissolves the body, the suffering of death presses upon them, and great fear arises. Therefore, meeting a good spiritual friend, they arouse great courage,
with mind after mind continuing for ten thoughts,
which is the augmenting root of good,
and so they attain rebirth
And if one takes
sound after sound without interruption
and "
with right mindfulness at death, a golden lotus comes to welcome
together with Master Shandao's teachings of "continuity brings rebirth" and "right mindfulness at death" (see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
article), then one clearly understands that Master Shandao, in the Commentary on the Four Fascicles of the Contemplation Sūtra, said
"provided one goes up to the whole of one life and down to ten thoughts, by the Buddha's vow-power, none are not reborn — hence it is called easy"
and
in the Praise of Rebirth (Wangsheng Lizan) said
"if I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions who call upon my name, down to ten sounds, if they are not reborn, may I not attain perfect enlightenment"
— the "down to ten thoughts" in these sentences
refers to the ten thoughts continuing without break at death

. But the Primal Vow teaching distorts this to mean the ten thoughts of a scattered mind reciting the Buddha at any time, and so concludes: Shandao says that calling the name ensures rebirth. This is a brazen distortion and slander of Master Shandao! (See the lecture "Master Shandao's Pure Land Thought" by Master Jingzong.)

[At the end of his life, he sees a golden lotus, like the disc of the sun, dwelling before him. In an instant of a single thought he is reborn in the land of utmost bliss. Within the lotus he is filled for twelve great kalpas, and only then does the lotus open. Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of great compassion, speak extensively to him of the true character of all dharmas, the Dharma that extinguishes offenses. Having heard it, he rejoices and at once arouses the bodhi-mind. This is called the lower grade, lower birth.]

At the end of his life this person sees a golden lotus, like the disc of the sun, dwelling before him. In an instant of a single thought he is reborn in the Western Pure Land. Within the lotus he remains for a full twelve great kalpas before the lotus opens. Then the bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, with voices of great compassion, speak extensively to him of the Dharma of extinguishing all offenses through the true character of all dharmas. Having heard it, he joyfully believes and receives it, and at once arouses the bodhi-mind. This is the lower grade, lower birth.
[The Dharma of extinguishing offenses through the true character of all dharmas]
The method of extinguishing all offenses through the true character of all dharmas. The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Practice of the Bodhisattva Universally Good says:

"All the seas of karmic hindrances arise from deluded thought. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true character. All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can melt them away."

[The true character of all dharmas] What is called "true character" is the actual state of things; "the true character of all dharmas" is the actual state of all dharmas. The Buddha-treasury Sūtra (Fozang Jing) says:
"What is called the true character of all dharmas? That is, all dharmas are ultimately empty, having nothing at all."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"All dharmas are like illusory marks; the Tathāgata dwelling within them, by his power of expedient means, is attached to nothing."
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"The great bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, in accord with the true character, without inversion, without agitation, without retreat, without turning."

[Arousing the bodhi-mind] Arousing the mind of enlightenment. "Bodhi" is translated into Chinese as "awakening." [Arousing the bodhi-mind] Its full name is "arousing the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi." The bodhi-mind is the intrinsically pure mind. This intrinsically pure mind is equal between sentient beings and Buddhas, present in everyone, neither increasing nor decreasing. "To arouse" means to set going, to develop, to unfold. To arouse the bodhi-mind is to set going and unfold the intrinsically pure mind. At the beginning the mind is merely aroused; upon seeing one's nature it is called unfolding. [Seeing one's nature] To see through to one's fundamental nature.

Question: The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says that even a person of the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds can be reborn in the Western Pure Land. Therefore the name ensures rebirth, and the salvation of Amitābha Buddha takes evil-doers as its proper target. Master Huijing, in his Essentials of Master Shandao, says: "Fail to understand that the purpose of the Contemplation Sūtra is to make manifest Amitābha's primal vow: evil-doers as the proper target." Master Xinyuan, a disciple of Master Huijing, says: "Let us now look — toward what kind of sentient being is Amitābha's salvation directed as its proper target? Evil-doers as the proper target." The Forty-Eight Sayings of Master Hōnen (also called the Sayings on Nianfo for Peace of Mind), compiled by Master Huijing, says: "The essential
heart

of the Pure Land school lies in this: no matter who it is, if one recites the Buddha one is reborn. Even an evil-doer without equal in the world, if he recites Namo Amitābha Buddha — even with a single thought — attains rebirth." It also says: "If a person commits the five grave offenses, then upon hearing the six-character name (hearing "Namo Amitābha Buddha"), the fire-chariot (the hellish fire-chariot) of itself departs, and the lotus platform comes to welcome him."

[The five grave offenses] The five grave offenses: five kinds of crimes at the utmost contrary to principle, namely killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing blood to flow from the Buddha's body, and splitting the harmonious Saṃgha. These five are deeds of extreme wickedness; the commission of any one causes one to fall into the Avīci hell, and so they are also called "the Avīci karma."

Answer: As stated above, in the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, a person of the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds is not one for whom calling the name ensures rebirth;
rather, he has accomplished the ten thoughts continuing without break at death and is reborn with the extinction of his offenses
In the passage on the lower grade, upper birth in the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life
it is said:

"At that time that Buddha straightway sends a transformation-Buddha, a transformation-Avalokiteshvara, and a transformation-Mahasthamaprapta before the practitioner, who praise him saying: "Well done! Good man,
because you called upon the Buddha's name, all your offenses are extinguished
, and so I have come to welcome you.""
Moreover, the purpose of the Contemplation Sūtra is not "to make manifest Amitābha's primal vow: evil-doers as the proper target." The commentary above contained such a passage; I repeat it here:
Please pay special attention to this passage:
"Thus with utmost sincerity, let the sound be unbroken, being complete in ten thoughts, calling upon "Namo Amitābha Buddha.""
In the passage,
thus with utmost sincerity
means there is no stray thought;
let the sound be unbroken
means the Buddha-name continues without interruption;
being complete in ten thoughts, calling upon "Namo Amitābha Buddha"
means having completed ten utterances of "Namo Amitābha Buddha." Because these three conditions are fulfilled — that is, having accomplished
the ten thoughts continuing without break at death
— only then does such an evil person attain
the extinction of
the offenses of birth and death of eighty koṭis of kalpas and be reborn in the Western Pure Land.
Originally, the "lower grade, lower birth" chapter of the Contemplation Sūtra speaks of the person thus reborn (a person of the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds who has accomplished
the ten thoughts continuing without break at death
and
extinguished his offenses
and been reborn) — his grade is the lower grade, lower birth.
The Primal Vow teaching, however, deliberately omits
the ten thoughts continuing without break at death

— this key point — and exaggerates it into the claim that all persons of the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds attain rebirth, thereby advocating "calling the name ensures rebirth" and the so-called "theory of the evil-doer as the proper target."
Moreover, at the very beginning of this sūtra (the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life), the Buddha teaches:
Those who wish to be reborn in that land
(the Western Pure Land)
should cultivate the three meritorious deeds

First, to be filial to one's parents, to serve one's teachers and elders, to be kind and not to kill, and to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds; second, to receive and hold the Three Refuges, to be complete in all the precepts, and not to violate dignified deportment; third, to arouse the bodhi-mind, to believe deeply in cause and effect, to recite and read the Mahāyāna, and to encourage and advance fellow practitioners."
In this passage the Buddha states it perfectly clearly: "
Those who wish to be reborn in that land
(the Western Pure Land)
should cultivate the three meritorious deeds.
How can it be that
the purpose of the Contemplation Sūtra is to make manifest Amitābha's primal vow: evil-doers as the proper target
This is nothing short of unbridled distortion!
And
moreover, our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha declared with his own golden mouth that the
Sūtra of Praise of the Pure Land, Embraced by the Buddhas
says:
"Sentient beings without abundant roots of good should not be reborn in the Pure Land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life's land of ultimate bliss."
(Translation: sentient beings with few roots of good do not attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land.) And in the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says:

"You should resolve of your own accord, keep your body upright and your conduct upright, and all the more do every kind of good. Cultivate yourself and purify your body, wash away the defilement of your heart. Let your words and deeds be loyal and trustworthy, and your outward and inward accord. A person can save himself, then in turn rescue and relieve others; with clear resolve he seeks the vow, accumulating the roots of good. Though he toils diligently for one life, in a brief moment afterward he is reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where joy is without limit."
And yet the Primal Vow teaching loudly proclaims "evil-doers as the proper target" — to such a degree it slanders the Buddha and destroys the Dharma!

[Roots of good] That is, the good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. Because they can produce excellent fruits, they are called roots. [Sentient beings] Also called living beings — all animals possessed of sentience.

Judge for yourself: do those who neither diligently and single-mindedly recite the Buddha, nor observe the precepts, nor cultivate merit, nor purify their own minds — and who even commit evil all their lives (including slandering the true Dharma) — possess such blessed virtue and such power of practice as to accomplish the ten thoughts continuing without break at death? If they cannot, then where will they go after death, and what will be the retribution of their future lives, life after life?

As for the person of the five grave offenses and ten evil deeds spoken of in the Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, why is it that at death he can meet a good spiritual friend who teaches him to recite the Buddha? Why can he at once joyfully believe and receive it, and with utmost sincerity call the name, accomplishing the ten thoughts continuing without break

It is because in his former lives he was already a practitioner with considerable power of practice, who, not having cut off the delusions of views and thought, has been revolving in saṃsāra down to this life. In this life he mistakenly took a wrong path and committed evil for a lifetime. At death, under the instruction of his good friend, he awakened all at once, repented with utmost sincerity, and accomplished the ten thoughts continuing without break and was reborn. Consider: if it were not founded on the bodhi-mind of former lives and on deep power of practice, then amid the pressing anguish of all suffering at death, how could he suddenly give rise to faith and vow and, all at once, accomplish the ten thoughts continuing without break?
On this point, the patriarchs and great masters of the Pure Land school through the ages have given many such instructions.
For example,
Master Ouyi
says
"The scripture says that those who committed the ten evil deeds and the five grave offenses attained rebirth. They
must have planted bodhi seeds in the past.
If there were no bodhi-seed, how could they meet a good friend? And even if they met a good friend who urged them on, how could they suddenly give rise to faith and vow and call upon the great name?"
(from the Collected Discourses of Ouyi on Lingfeng, the General Sermon at Tianma Monastery, Shepu)
Master Ouyi also says:
The ten thoughts at death
must be founded on deep roots of good.
Now if with the advent of adverse and favorable circumstances one no longer has right mindfulness
(the recitation-thought without mixed deluded thought)

, how much less at death? Moreover, at death when suffering appears one relies only on the good friend's reminder; yet now in broad daylight, when all is bright, one still cannot believe and practice the genuine, true counsel of an enlightened teacher and good friend!"
(from the Collected Discourses of Ouyi on Lingfeng
Preface to the Cultivation of the Pure Land Repentance and the Society for Releasing Life)

Translation: To accomplish the ten thoughts that continue without break at death, one must be deeply rooted in good. Now if, once adverse and favorable circumstances arise, one no longer has right mindfulness
(the recitation-thought without mixed deluded thought)

, how much more can one maintain right mindfulness at death? Moreover, now in broad daylight, when all is bright and clear, one still cannot believe and practice the genuine exhortation and instruction of an enlightened teacher and good friend — so how can one vainly hope that at the moment of death, merely relying on the good friend's reminder and instruction, one will be able to believe and practice it?
